To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
1) the VAE objective is biased towards learning a higher dimensional manifold than the ground truth, and 2) this is due to the implicit bias of gradient-based optimization.

(i) VAE training with linear encoders/linear decoders recovers a generator with support on the ground truth lower dimensional manifold; (ii) VAE training frequently recovers a generator which has support equal to a higher dimensional superset of the manifold.

the VAE loss has an implicit bias towards learning a lower dimensional manifold, and this implicit bias is not always strong enough to overcome the tendency of gradient descent to overfit to the data.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
VAE training is a good way to learn a low-dimensional manifold when the data is supported on a linear one, but not otherwise.
the VAE training dynamics are more complex than previously thought, and that in the nonlinear case, the generator does not converge to the ground truth.
VAEs do not necessarily recover the ground truth manifold, but that the training dynamics do have an implicit bias to do so.
The main takeaway from our work is that
in the presence of a low-dimensional manifold, VAE training is implicitly biased towards a generator which learns a superset of that manifold, rather than the ground truth manifold itself.
VAE training is a highly complex process, and that the implicit bias of gradient flow on the VAE loss landscape is a major factor that determines the learned manifold.
VAE training is not guaranteed to find the true manifold and that the implicit bias of gradient flow can be exploited to improve VAE training.
